note: Governance as code with signed evidence artifacts and clause level traceability across EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and ISO 42001.
title: From Policy to Pipeline: A Governance Framework for AI Development and Operations Pipelines
explain_beginner: Checking whether an AI system follows the rules, safety testing, documentation, sign off before release, is usually done by people writing reports after the system is mostly built, which is slow and easy to skip under deadline pressure. This paper proposes doing that checking automatically, inside the same software pipeline that trains and deploys the AI, so compliance is enforced as code rather than reviewed afterward on paper. The system, called GEAP, places automatic checkpoints at five points in an AI project's life, when data is collected, when the model is trained, when it is validated, when it is released, and while it is running in production, and at each checkpoint it generates a signed, tamper resistant record proving what was checked and what passed. The authors demonstrate this on a hospital early warning system that flags patients at risk of sepsis, showing the approach can automatically produce the kind of evidence regulators ask for. Whether this approach works as well outside that one healthcare example is not yet shown.
explain_business: For a regulated organization building AI, healthcare, finance, critical infrastructure, this approach points toward treating compliance evidence as a byproduct of the engineering pipeline itself rather than a separate paperwork exercise done before an audit, which in principle cuts the manual work of proving compliance across multiple frameworks at once and produces tamper evident records that are harder to dispute during a regulatory review. Since the demonstrated case is a healthcare early warning system, organizations in other sectors should treat this as a promising direction rather than an off the shelf solution, the specific gates and metrics were validated in one domain and would need adaptation and its own validation before being trusted for, say, a lending model or an industrial control system. The relevant condition for this to matter now is having enough in house pipeline engineering capacity to build these controls, since GEAP describes an architecture to adopt, not a purchasable product.
explain_practitioner: GEAP, short for Governance Evidence for AI Pipelines, implements governance as executable code enforced at five gates across an ML pipeline, Data, Training, Validation, Release, and Operations, each producing signed, content addressed artifacts stored in what the authors call an Evidence Backbone. These artifacts are automatically mapped to specific clauses in the EU AI Act, NIST's AI Risk Management Framework, and ISO/IEC 42001, replacing manual documentation with deterministic traceability, and the framework also computes governance metrics for adequacy, completeness, stability, and evidence quality. The validation case is a sepsis early warning system, where the authors show GEAP enforcing promotion policies, catching rule violations, and producing an audit ready compliance bundle without manual effort. The clear limitation is scope, the published validation rests on this single clinical case study, so how the five gate model and its metrics hold up across different regulatory regimes, data types, or industries outside healthcare has not yet been demonstrated in the paper.
